In galaxies where our line of sight passes through an edgeon or close to edge-on disk of molecular gas, we find low velocity dispersion clouds (typically <9 km/s) with no net inflow our outflow (Figures 14 and 15).

When excluding disks, we find that absorption regions have significantly different properties. They have wide velocity dispersions (typically >9 km/s), and in terms of their line of sight velocities, appear to split into two groups.

We find a wide range in the CO(2-1)/CO(1-0) ratios of the absorption regions. In around half of cases, the ratio implies a nonphysical negative excitation temperature. We show that the high CO(2-1)/CO(1-0) ratios can be explained by variation in the structure of the continuum source with frequency, combined with substructure in the molecular clouds.

all_quotes.loc: 4.1 Velocity distribution of molecular absorption lines – evidence of cold gas inflow
all_quotes.quote: In Figure 15, we also show the infall velocity of the absorption regions versus their velocity dispersion. This shows two distinct populations of molecular clouds. In disks, we see narrow absorption features with no net movement towards the galaxy centre.

When excluding disks, we find that absorption regions have significantly different properties. They have wide velocity dispersions (typically >9 km/s), and in terms of their line of sight velocities, appear to split into two groups.

In galactic cores, we find high velocity dispersion clouds inflowing at up to 550 km/s. This provides observational evidence in favour of cold accretion onto galactic centres, which likely contributes to the fuelling of active galactic nuclei.

If the CO(1-0) excitation temperature is 20 K and the CO(2-1) excitation temperature is 5 K, then a ratio in the velocity integrated optical depths of 5.6 is expected. This temperature difference is at the more extreme end of what could be expected, but is still far from explaining the ratios of over 10 which we see in the absorption lines of some systems.

Instead, a continuum that changes in size with frequency, combined with the hierarchical structure of the molecular clouds, could explain the otherwise impossible CO(2-1)/CO(1-0) molecular line ratios.
